lead: Every 3D interface begins with what the user can physically do, and that comes from the input device. A device turns a hand movement or a button press into numbers the program reads. We judge it by how many independent motions it reports, how those motions map to the task, and what the hand feels while using it. Desktop devices such as the mouse, joystick, keyboard and touchscreen are the baseline: every VR controller is compared against them, and most VR systems still use them for setup and menus. This chapter defines those measures, then applies them to desktop and special purpose devices.
prereq: You need Unit 1, for where input sits among the components of a VR system.

sections.h3: An input device and its degrees of freedom

blocks.text: An input device turns a user's action into data a program can read: a position, a rate, a button state or a hand shape. The same small set of characteristics describes every device, so a VR controller and an office mouse can be compared on equal terms.

Degrees of freedom (DOF) is the number of independent motions the device reports. A mouse has 2 DOF, left-right and forward-back on the desk. A 6-DOF device reports three translations (x, y, z) and three rotations (yaw, pitch, roll). DOF counts motions, not buttons: a mouse with three buttons still has 2 DOF of motion.

An absolute device reports where it is inside its own workspace; a touchscreen knows the finger is at a fixed spot on the glass. A relative device reports only how far it moved since the last reading, like a mouse. Absolute readings map straight to a position. Relative readings must be added up, and a lost reading is lost for good.

In position control the device's displacement sets the object's position: move the mouse 3 cm and the cursor jumps a fixed number of pixels. In rate control the displacement sets a velocity: push the joystick further and the viewpoint moves faster. Position control is zero-order, rate control first-order, and acceleration control (second-order) is harder to learn. Chapter 2.3 applies this to travel.

sections.h3: Isotonic, isometric and elastic; and quality measures

blocks.text: Devices also differ in what the hand feels.

items: Isotonic: moves with the hand and measures displacement, like a mouse or a pen. Proprioception, the body's sense of limb position, tells the user where it is, so the eyes stay on the screen.
Isometric: hardly moves and measures force, like a stiff force stick or a spaceball. Workspace is unlimited because nothing travels, but the hand gets no position cue.
Elastic: moves a little against a spring and measures that small displacement, like a self-centering joystick that returns to the middle when released.
Resolution: the smallest change reported, such as counts per inch.
Accuracy: closeness of the reading to the true value. Precision: how tightly repeated readings cluster, right or wrong.
Repeatability: the same action twice gives the same reading.
Latency: delay from action to system, in milliseconds. Update rate: readings per second, in hertz, so 120 Hz is one reading every 8.3 ms.
Jitter: how much the latency varies between readings.
Workspace, fatigue and cost in rupees.

Mouse: 2 DOF, relative, isotonic, position control. Resolution runs to thousands of counts per inch and the buttons give discrete input. It runs out of desk, so the user lifts and repositions; the lift reports nothing, which is exactly what relative reporting tolerates.
Trackball: the same 2 DOF, but the ball is fixed and the hand rolls it. No desk travel is needed, which helps on a crowded desk; fine pointing is harder for many users.
Touchpad: 2 DOF, relative and indirect, because the finger's place on the pad is not the cursor's place on the screen.
Joystick: 2 or 3 DOF, elastic and self-centering. Good as a rate control for steering, poor for picking a small target.
Spaceball: 6 DOF, isometric. Push, pull and twist with almost no travel. Good for turning a 3D model, weak for accurate translation.
Keyboard: discrete keys only, no analogue motion, still the fastest text entry. Touchscreen: absolute and direct, natural pointing, but the finger covers the target and resolution is coarse.
3D mice: a 6-DOF puck reports six motions per sample. Some syllabi call these special purpose input devices. Two-handed use, puck in one hand and mouse in the other, is common in CAD.

sections.h3: Selecting a device for a 3D interface

items: Write the task in one line: select a target, steer continuously, or enter text.
Decide discrete or continuous. A menu choice wants a button or a key; steering wants an analogue axis.
Choose position or rate control by distance and precision. Short precise moves want position control; long travel wants rate control.
Count the DOF the task needs, then add feedback only if the task needs it.
Check latency, update rate, jitter, workspace, fatigue and cost against the budget.
Test on the real task with a few users; if it fails, go back to step one.

spec.aria: Timeline of one 16.7 millisecond display frame carrying two tracker samples, the first at 0 and the second at 8.3 milliseconds, so two samples arrive per frame.

examples.question: A VR cricket game renders 60 frames per second, so one frame lasts 16.7 ms. The bat tracker samples at 120 Hz. (a) How many tracker samples arrive per frame? (b) The menu cursor is driven by a mouse with 800 counts per inch; the user slides it 1.5 inches. How many counts is that? (c) How many DOF must the bat tracker report?
steps: Frame period T = 1/60 s = 0.0167 s = 16.7 ms.
Tracker period = 1/120 s = 0.0083 s = 8.3 ms, so two tracker readings fit inside one frame.
Samples per frame = 120 Hz × 0.0167 s = 2.0, which is the same as 120 ÷ 60.
DOF = 3 translations (x, y, z of the bat) + 3 rotations (its swing angles) = 6 DOF.
examples.answer: Two tracker samples per frame, 1200 counts for the 1.5 inch slide, and 6 DOF for the bat tracker.
examples.check:
fps = 60
rate_hz = 120
cpi = 800
inches = 1.5

samples_per_frame = rate_hz * (1.0 / fps)
counts = int(cpi * inches)
dof = 3 + 3

print(round(samples_per_frame, 2))
print(counts)
print(dof)

code.code:
fps = 60
rate = 120
samples = round(rate / fps, 2)
counts = int(800 * 1.5)
dof = 3 + 3
print(samples)
print(counts)
print(dof)

examples.question: A tracker samples at 90 Hz and the display runs at 72 frames per second. How many tracker samples arrive per frame, and why does the number matter for the user?
steps: Samples per frame = tracker rate ÷ frame rate.
So some frames get one sample and some get two; the pose used on screen is at most one sample old.
The mismatch shows up as uneven motion, which the user feels as jitter even though the average rate is fine.
examples.answer: 1.25 samples per frame, meaning some frames reuse the previous pose.

traps: DOF counts independent motions, not buttons or sensors. A mouse has 2 DOF of motion and three buttons; a 6-DOF puck has six motions and often no useful button.
A mouse reports relative movement, so it has no absolute position to hand to a tracker. Never quote mouse readings as world coordinates.
Isotonic and isometric are swapped easily. Isotonic means the device moves with the hand, isometric means it measures force with almost no movement.
Update rate is not latency. A 120 Hz device with 40 ms latency and heavy jitter feels worse than a steady 60 Hz device.
Repeatability is not accuracy: a device can return the same wrong value every single time.

quiz.q: Define degrees of freedom for an input device and state the DOF of a mouse.
quiz.a: The number of independent motions the device reports. A mouse reports 2, left-right and forward-back.

quiz.q: What is an isometric input device? Give one example.
quiz.a: A device that measures force while hardly moving, such as a spaceball or a stiff force-sensing stick.

quiz.q: Why does relative reporting survive the lift-and-reposition of a mouse?
quiz.a: The lift produces no counts, so no jump is added; only movement while the mouse rests on the surface is counted.
Resolution is the smallest change reported. Accuracy is closeness to the true value. Precision is how tightly repeated readings cluster, whether or not they are correct.

quiz.q: A tracker samples at 90 Hz and the display runs at 72 frames per second. How many samples arrive per frame?
A mouse reports 1000 counts per inch and one count moves the cursor one pixel. How far must the hand move to cross a 1500-pixel screen?
quiz.a: 1500 pixels ÷ 1000 counts per inch = 1.5 inches of hand movement.

quiz.q: Why is a self-centering joystick a poor choice for picking a small icon but a good one for long travel?
quiz.a: It acts as rate control with a spring, so speed follows push and there is no absolute position; fine aiming is hard. But its displacement never runs out, so long travel is easy.

quiz.q: Device A has 10 ms latency, 1 ms jitter and 400 counts per inch. Device B has 25 ms latency, 12 ms jitter and 2000 counts per inch. Which do you pick for aiming at a moving target, and why?
quiz.a: Device A. Low latency and low jitter keep the cursor steady under the hand; extra resolution is wasted when each reading arrives late and by an unpredictable amount.

beyond: Not for the exam. Commercial VR controllers are 6-DOF pucks with trigger and grip buttons, and their pose comes from inertial sensors fused with camera or lighthouse data. Modern engines hide the hardware behind an action-based input layer, as in OpenXR, so one grab action can come from a controller, a hand tracker or a mouse. Search next for OpenXR action sets, Fitts's law for 3D pointing, throughput measured in bits per second, and the ISO 9241 pointing-device standards.
